name: Bromeliads and tillandsias — archetypal set
status: 8 archetypal species (full list archived in docs/plant_archive)
notes: Nearly all-American family. Tillandsias are air plants: rootless, grey, drinking fog and rain, hanging from anything (Spanish moss curtains are the reference look for swamp oaks). Tank bromeliads hold water in their leaf cups — tree frogs and mosquito larvae breed in them, so a tank counts as a nest site and a tiny pond for the insect ledger. Ground rosettes (bromelia, puya, hechtia) are spined and make natural hedges; camp folk use them as living fences. Puya raimondii is a landmark plant that flowers once a century.

shrub.name: Queen of the Andes

growth.juvenile_note: For decades a stemless, ever-widening ball of stiff, narrow, grey-green leaves (to 1-1.25 m long) with hooked spines on the edges. Later a thick trunk up to 4 m lifts the rosette, skirted by a shaggy thatch of dead leaves. At the end a colossal spike 4-8 m tall bursts from the centre carrying thousands of flowers; after seeding the whole plant dies.
growth.source: Wikipedia Puya raimondii (flowers at 40-100 yr in the wild, 28 yr at UC Botanical Garden Berkeley; trunk to 4 m; leaves 1-1.25 m; spike 4-8 m with 8,000-20,000 flowers and ~12 million seeds; 2,400-4,200 m); germination and trunk age estimated from Puya growers

repro.note: most bloom once then die, leaving pups; hummingbird-pollinated; tank species hold rainwater that frogs and insects breed in

shrub.source: Peruvian and Bolivian puna. Largest bromeliad; a 10 m spike once in a century, then dies. Kew POWO.

ground.name: Bromelia

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are small rosettes of narrow leaves already edged with hooked spines. They grow into big, fierce rosettes of long arching leaves with curved spines; at flowering the centre turns bright red. Each rosette flowers once and dies, but stolons build dense, impenetrable colonies.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Mexico, Central America, West Indies; planted as a spiny living fence; fruit used for gruel); bromeliad growers' data (seed germination 1-4 weeks; rosettes flower once then die); timings estimated. lifespan_years is the rosette.

epiphyte.name: Spanish moss

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are minute grey tufts of thread-like leaves on bark, but most new plants start as windblown or bird-carried fragments. A young plant is a short, curly chain of silvery-grey scaly stems with 2-6 cm thread leaves, lengthening over years into festoons that hang 1-6 m (rarely 8 m) from branches, with tiny three-petalled flowers in spring.
growth.source: Wikipedia Spanish moss (leaves 2-6 cm x 1 mm; hanging festoons to 6 m, rarely 8 m; spreads by seed and by fragments carried by wind and nesting birds; small flowers with spreading petals). Seed germination, strand growth rate, first flowering and festoon age estimated.

epiphyte.name: Ball moss

growth.juvenile_note: Plumed seeds stick to twigs, bark and even power lines; the seedling is a tiny grey tuft of thin, curved, scaly leaves. Shoots branch as they grow, so within a few years a young plant becomes a spiky grey tuft and then a round ball of many recurved shoots, golf-ball to soccer-ball size, each sending up a thin stalk with one or two small pale-violet flowers.
growth.source: Wikipedia Tillandsia recurvata (ball moss: balls golf-ball to soccer-ball size made of many joined shoots; seeds plentiful, with fine hairs; southern USA to Argentina and Chile; favours humid, sheltered sites; frost-sensitive). Flowering age, growth and ball lifespan estimated.

epiphyte.name: Air plant

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are pin-head tufts of a few silvery, scaly, needle-like leaves on bark or rock and take years to reach a few centimetres. The adult is a compact 4-10 cm rosette of stiff, curved, silvery-green leaves; at flowering the inner leaves blush bright red and violet tubular flowers with yellow stamens poke out, then it pups into dense clumps.
growth.source: Bromeliad literature (T. ionantha: small atmospheric epiphyte of Mexico and Central America on trees and rocks; inner leaves redden at flowering; violet tubular flowers visited by hummingbirds; clumps by offsets, each rosette flowering once). Seed-to-flower time (~5 yr) and rosette lifespan estimated from growers.

epiphyte.name: Rock tillandsia

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are tiny white fuzzballs of thin leaves wrapped in long silvery trichomes, clinging to rock or cactus on dry Andean slopes. The adult is a round rosette 10-20 cm across of narrow leaves so densely feathered with white hairs it looks frosted, like a snowball; it flowers once with a pink bracted spike of lilac flowers, then pups into a clump.
growth.source: Bromeliad literature (T. tectorum: lithophyte and epiphyte of dry, sunny Andean slopes of Ecuador and Peru; leaves with exceptionally long white trichomes; pink bracts and violet-blue flowers; offsets after flowering). Growth, flowering age and rosette lifespan estimated from bromeliad horticulture.

epiphyte.name: Tank bromeliad

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are tiny tufts of thin, narrow, grass-like leaves; by year 2-3 they form an urn-shaped tank rosette of broad, arching, silver-banded grey-green leaves with spiny edges. Each rosette flowers once (a pink bracted spike) and then slowly dies over a year or two while 1-3 pups grow from its base.
growth.source: Bromeliad growers' guides (seed germinates in 1-4 weeks; seed-grown plants flower in about 3-5 years; rosettes die after flowering and pup); Bromeliads.info Aechmea fasciata growing guide

epiphyte.name: Guzmania
epiphyte.origin: Central America and northern S America

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-fine plumed seeds lodge on bark and moss; seedlings are tiny grass-like tufts of thin green leaves that slowly widen into a glossy, strap-leaved tank rosette. After ~3-4 years the rosette flowers once (a star of scarlet/orange bracts around small white flowers), makes offsets (pups) at its base, and then slowly dies.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Guzmania lingulata: epiphytic tank bromeliad of Central and South American rainforests, orange-red bracted inflorescence); bromeliad horticulture (monocarpic rosettes, seed to flower in ~2-4 yr, pups after flowering). Values estimated.
